title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
pattern: DFS with memoization / longest path on a DAG
statement:
You are given a rectangular integer matrix `matrix` with `m` rows and `n` columns. A path is a sequence of cells in which each consecutive pair shares an edge (up, down, left or right, never diagonal) and no cell appears twice. The path is strictly increasing when the value in every cell is strictly greater than the value in the cell before it.

Return the number of cells on the longest strictly increasing path. A single cell counts as a path of length 1, so the answer is always at least 1.

For example, in `[[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]]` the path `1 -> 2 -> 6 -> 9` uses four cells and no longer strictly increasing path exists, so the answer is 4. In `[[1, 1], [1, 1]]` every neighbour is equal, so the answer is 1.

Constraints: `1 <= matrix.length <= 30` and `1 <= matrix[i].length <= 30` and `-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Draw an edge from a cell to any edge-neighbour holding a strictly larger value. Every edge points from a smaller value to a larger one, so the graph has no cycle and you are looking for the longest path in it.

The best path starting at a cell is that cell followed by the best path starting at one of its larger neighbours. Turn that sentence into a recurrence and evaluate it with memoization so each cell is computed once.
If you would rather not recurse, set every cell's length to 1 and sweep the entire grid repeatedly, extending each cell from its strictly smaller neighbours, until a full sweep changes nothing.

editorial.approach: Give every cell a path length of 1 and sweep the whole grid repeatedly, extending a cell from any edge-neighbour whose value is strictly smaller: if that neighbour already supports a path of length L, the current cell can support L + 1. Repeat full sweeps until a sweep changes nothing, which is the Bellman-Ford relaxation idea applied to an acyclic graph, and costs O((m * n)^2) in the worst case. The memoized DFS removes the repetition: the answer for a cell depends only on its larger neighbours, so it never changes once computed. Cache it on first visit and each cell is expanded exactly once, giving O(m * n).
editorial.why_optimal: Every cell must be inspected and compared against up to four neighbours, so O(m * n) time and O(m * n) space for the memo table is the floor; a cell that might extend a path cannot be skipped. The relaxation version needs no memo table but pays a multiplicative factor of (m * n), and the 30 by 30 bound keeps that small enough to run as a reference implementation.
editorial.pitfalls: Using a non-strict comparison: a plateau of equal values must break the chain, and allowing equal neighbours turns a cycle into an infinite recursion instead of a finite graph. Reading the memo table as a boolean: a computed answer of 1 must still count as visited, so the sentinel has to be 0 and the check has to be a length comparison. In the relaxation version, stopping after one sweep under-reports staircases such as `[[3, 2, 1]]`, where the longest path runs against the scan order. Deep recursion can nest as deep as the number of cells, which a fully ordered 30 by 30 grid makes real.
